note:
Dictating a follow up visit in the psychiatry specialty clinic for a 69-year-old female with schizophrenia who is stable on a long-acting injectable. She works rotating shifts at a hospital laundry, so her schedule is irregular, and she came in today straight off a night shift, tired but cooperative and well groomed. She was anxious throughout the visit and asked a great many questions, mainly whether the injection could interact with her other pills, whether she still needs it now that she feels well, and what would happen if she missed a dose because of work.

Interval history. She denies auditory hallucinations, denies paranoid thoughts, denies command voices, and denies any thoughts of harming herself or others. She says her sleep is broken by the shift rotation, about five hours on work days, with daytime sleepiness after night shifts. She denies tremor, denies stiffness, and denies restlessness. She reports mild constipation and occasional dry mouth. No falls since the last visit. She denies alcohol and drug use. Adherence has been good and she has not missed an injection.

Medications as she reported them. She first told me her injection is paliperidone palmitate 234 mg IM monthly, correction, I checked the clinic administration record and the dose is 156 mg IM every four weeks, last given four weeks ago, so 156 mg is the correct dose. She also takes metformin 1000 mg BID for type 2 diabetes, lisinopril 10 mg daily for hypertension, atorvastatin 40 mg nightly for hyperlipidemia, and benztropine 1 mg BID which was started years ago for stiffness. No known drug allergies.

Examination and data. Blood pressure 152/88, heart rate 74, weight 78 kg. On mental status exam she is alert, speech normal in rate, mood described as nervous, affect anxious but congruent, thought process linear, no delusions elicited, not responding to internal stimuli, insight and judgment fair. AIMS score is 2, no tardive dyskinesia, no rigidity or cogwheeling on exam. ECG today shows normal sinus rhythm with QTc 438 ms. Labs from last week show A1c 7.2 percent, fasting glucose 118, creatinine 1.0 with eGFR 68, and LDL 96.

Impression. Schizophrenia, stable, with no positive symptoms on paliperidone palmitate. Hypertension not at goal today, probably worsened by sleep loss after a night shift. Type 2 diabetes with an A1c of 7.2 percent, acceptable for her age. Hyperlipidemia with LDL at goal. Shift work sleep disorder. Benztropine is no longer needed because she has no extrapyramidal symptoms and it likely contributes to the constipation and dry mouth.

Recommendations. Continue paliperidone palmitate 156 mg IM every four weeks and schedule the injections on her days off, and we will discuss the three-month formulation at the next visit to reduce the number of trips. Stop benztropine today. Increase lisinopril from 10 mg to 20 mg daily and recheck blood pressure and a BMP in two weeks. Start melatonin 3 mg before daytime sleep after night shifts. Continue metformin 1000 mg BID and atorvastatin 40 mg nightly. Repeat A1c and a lipid panel in three months. I answered her questions one by one, explained that stopping the injection raises the risk of relapse, and gave her a written calendar of injection dates and a crisis line to call if the voices return. Return to clinic in four weeks for the next injection and in three months for a full visit.
summary: A 69-year-old female with schizophrenia stable on paliperidone palmitate attended psychiatry follow-up after a night shift, anxious and asking many questions. She denied hallucinations, paranoid thoughts, command voices and thoughts of harming herself or others, and reported broken sleep from rotating shifts, mild constipation and dry mouth. Blood pressure was 152/88, AIMS score was 2, QTc was 438 ms, A1c was 7.2 percent and eGFR was 68. The assessment was stable schizophrenia, hypertension not at goal, type 2 diabetes, hyperlipidemia and shift work sleep disorder. Paliperidone palmitate 156 mg continues every four weeks, benztropine was stopped, lisinopril was increased to 20 mg, and melatonin was started.

note:
Nurse: Triage note for the 67-year-old male in bed four. Left flank pain that started about three hours ago, rated nine out of ten, and he vomited once in the waiting room. Blood pressure 158/94, heart rate 98, temp 98.6, oxygen sat 98% on room air.

Doctor: Hello, I'm the emergency doctor. Tell me what happened.

Patient: It came on out of nowhere. Sharp pain in my left side, and it shoots down toward my groin. I can't sit still, I keep pacing.

Doctor: Any fever or chills?

Patient: No fever, no chills.

Doctor: Any burning when you urinate, or blood in the urine?

Patient: No burning. The urine looked a little pink this morning, though.

Doctor: Have you ever had a kidney stone before?

Patient: Never.

Doctor: Have you traveled recently?

Patient: I flew back from Thailand three days ago, about a seventeen hour trip, and it was really hot there. I wasn't drinking much water.

Doctor: Did you have any diarrhea or a stomach bug while you were away?

Patient: No diarrhea, I was careful with what I ate.

Doctor: What medicines do you take?

Patient: Just amlodipine 5 mg once a day for my blood pressure. No allergies to medicines.

Doctor: Okay. On exam you look uncomfortable, you have tenderness over the left flank, and your belly is soft with no guarding. Your urine test shows blood but no sign of infection. The CT scan without contrast shows a 5 mm stone in the upper left ureter with mild hydronephrosis, which means some backup of urine into the kidney. Your creatinine is 1.2 and your white count is 9.8, so the kidney is working fine and there is no sign of infection. This is renal colic from a kidney stone. The nurse gave you ketorolac 15 mg IV and ondansetron 4 mg IV for the pain and nausea.

Patient: The pain is already down to a three.

Doctor: Good. I want to start tamsulosin 0.4 mg once daily to help the stone pass, and ibuprofen 600 mg every 6 hours with food for pain. Keep taking your amlodipine. Drink plenty of water and strain your urine to catch the stone. You need to see urology in about a week. Come straight back if you get a fever, uncontrolled pain, repeated vomiting, or if you can't pass urine.

Patient: Okay, thank you.
summary: A 67-year-old male came to the emergency department with sudden left flank pain after returning from a long trip to Thailand three days earlier. He denied fever, chills, burning on urination and diarrhea, but vomited once and noticed a little pink urine. Left flank tenderness was present, urinalysis showed blood without infection, and CT showed a 5 mm left ureteral stone with mild hydronephrosis, with creatinine 1.2 and white count 9.8. The diagnosis was renal colic from a kidney stone, and pain fell to three out of ten after IV ketorolac and ondansetron. The plan is tamsulosin and ibuprofen, continued amlodipine, fluids with urine straining, urology follow-up in a week, and return precautions.

note:
Dermatology follow-up seen on the hospital ward for a 33-year-old male admitted three days ago with a left leg deep vein thrombosis, currently receiving apixaban 10 mg twice daily. The inpatient team asked for evaluation of facial redness and bumps that have been present for about two years and have worsened since admission. He describes flushing of the cheeks and nose with hot drinks and stress, along with intermittent stinging. He denies eye pain, denies blurred vision, and denies itching or fever.

On examination there is central facial erythema with scattered inflammatory papules and a few pustules over the cheeks, nose, and chin, and visible telangiectasias on both cheeks. No comedones are seen. There is no rhinophyma and the conjunctivae are clear. The patient is hemodynamically stable per the primary team.

The impression is papulopustular rosacea. Topical therapy is preferred while he is hospitalized and anticoagulated, so I started azelaic acid 15% gel twice daily to the affected areas of the face. I counseled him on gentle skin care, daily broad-spectrum sunscreen, and avoiding triggers such as hot drinks and alcohol. Laser treatment of the telangiectasias will be deferred until he is no longer on apixaban. Apixaban will continue at 10 mg twice daily per the primary team. He will follow up in the dermatology clinic in six weeks to assess his response.
summary: A 33-year-old male on the hospital ward with a left leg deep vein thrombosis on apixaban was evaluated for two years of facial redness and bumps that worsened during admission. He reported flushing and intermittent stinging and denied eye pain, blurred vision, itching and fever. Examination showed central facial erythema, inflammatory papules and pustules, and telangiectasias without comedones or rhinophyma. The impression was papulopustular rosacea. Azelaic acid 15% gel twice daily was started, laser treatment is deferred while he is on apixaban, apixaban continues, and clinic follow-up is planned in six weeks.

57-year-old male, hospital day 2. Admitted w/ symptomatic hyponatremia, thiazide suspected.
Overnight: got 3% saline 100 mL bolus x1 in ED for confusion + nausea. No seizure. No vomiting. Neuro checks q4h unremarkable.
Today c/o mild HA + nausea, both better than on admission. Confusion resolved, A&O x3. Denies CP, denies SOB, denies focal weakness, denies diarrhea, denies excess water intake. ROS otherwise neg.
PMH: HTN, hyperlipidemia.
Social: denies EtOH, never smoker.
PTA meds: HCTZ 25 mg daily (started by PCP ~3 wks ago), lisinopril 20 mg daily, atorvastatin 20 mg nightly. NKDA.
Vitals: BP 154/92, HR 84, RR 16, Temp 98.2 F, SpO2 97% RA. Wt stable.
Exam: NAD, MMM, no JVD, no LE edema, lungs CTAB, abd soft NT, neuro nonfocal, no asterixis. Looks euvolemic.
Labs: Na 118 on admission -> 124 after bolus -> 126 this AM. K 3.9, Cr 0.9, glucose 102. Serum osm 258, urine osm 460. TSH 2.1. AM cortisol nl.
CXR: no infiltrate, no mass.
Hyponatremia w/u: no new meds or supplements besides HCTZ, no recent GI losses, no heavy beer or water intake.
Impression: symptomatic hyponatremia 2/2 thiazide (HCTZ), euvolemic. Rise so far is within safe limit. HTN above goal off diuretic. Hyperlipidemia stable.
Orders:
- D/c HCTZ, avoid thiazides going forward
- Fluid restrict 1.2 L/day
- BMP q6h, limit correction to 8 mEq/L in 24h, call MD if overcorrecting
- Start amlodipine 5 mg daily for BP, cont lisinopril 20 mg daily
- Cont atorvastatin 20 mg nightly
- Neuro checks q4h
- Regular diet w/ fluid restriction, SCDs for VTE ppx, full code
Dispo: remain on med-surg, likely d/c in 1-2 days if asymptomatic.
F/u PCP in 1 wk w/ BMP. Plan reviewed w/ pt, verbalized understanding.

He is euvolemic with sodium rising from 118 to 126, and blood pressure was 154/92. The assessment is thiazide-induced hyponatremia with a safe rate of rise, hypertension above goal, and stable hyperlipidemia. HCTZ is stopped, fluids restricted to 1.2 L per day, amlodipine started, BMP checked every 6 hours, and PCP follow-up is arranged in a week.

note:
Doctor: Good to see you again. For the record, I'm seeing a 54-year-old male for his COPD maintenance follow-up. How have you been since the last visit?

Patient: Not great, honestly. I still get winded going up the stairs at work, and the cough in the morning hasn't gone away.

Doctor: Tell me about the cough. Is it dry, or are you bringing up phlegm?

Patient: A spoonful of white phlegm in the morning, that's about it. No blood.

Doctor: Any fever, chills, or night sweats?

Patient: No fever, no chills, no night sweats.

Doctor: Any chest pain, or swelling in your ankles?

Patient: No chest pain and my ankles are fine. I do get a little wheeze at night when I lie flat, though.

Doctor: Any flare-ups since we last met?

Patient: Two in the past year. Both times I went to urgent care and they gave me steroids and an antibiotic. The second one was about two months ago.

Doctor: Which maintenance inhaler are you using, and how often?

Patient: The Anoro Ellipta, one puff every morning. I almost never miss it.

Doctor: And your rescue inhaler?

Patient: Albuterol, two puffs when I need it. I'd say once or twice a day.

Doctor: What else are you taking, including anything over the counter?

Patient: Lisinopril 10 mg once a day for hypertension, omeprazole 20 mg once a day for reflux, and atorvastatin 20 mg at night for high cholesterol. Over the counter I take fish oil, vitamin D, and a herbal lung support capsule from the health food store.

Doctor: How much vitamin D do you take?

Patient: 5,000 units a day. Hold on, let me check the bottle photo on my phone. No, it's 2,000 units daily. The 5,000 one was what I took last winter.

Doctor: Good, thank you for checking. What is in the herbal lung support capsule?

Patient: It lists mullein, ginseng, and licorice root. I take two capsules a day.

Doctor: Okay. Licorice root can raise blood pressure and lower potassium, so I would like you to stop that one. Do you still smoke?

Patient: No, I quit two years ago. I smoked about thirty pack-years.

Doctor: Good for you. Now your results. Vitals today: blood pressure 138/84, heart rate 82, respiratory rate 18, and oxygen saturation 94% on room air. On exam you have a prolonged expiratory phase and scattered expiratory wheezes, no crackles, and no leg edema. Your spirometry today shows a post-bronchodilator FEV1 of 52% of predicted and an FEV1 to FVC ratio of 0.58, about the same as last year. Your blood eosinophil count last week was 320, and the chest X-ray last month showed hyperinflation without any pneumonia.

Patient: So what does that mean?

Doctor: It means your COPD is moderate to severe, and with two flare-ups in a year despite dual therapy, plus the high eosinophils, you will benefit from a stronger inhaler. Your reflux can also make the cough worse, so we will increase the omeprazole.

Patient: Will the new inhaler interact with anything?

Doctor: No, not with your current medicines. Here is the plan. Stop the Anoro Ellipta and start Trelegy Ellipta, one inhalation once daily, and rinse your mouth afterward. Continue albuterol as needed. Increase omeprazole from 20 mg to 40 mg once daily. Stop the licorice herbal capsule, and you can continue the fish oil and the vitamin D at 2,000 units daily. I am referring you to pulmonary rehabilitation, ordering a yearly low-dose CT scan of the chest for lung cancer screening, and giving you a flu shot today. We will repeat spirometry in three months.

Patient: And if I get another flare-up?

Doctor: Call us the same day instead of waiting for urgent care. I will see you back in three months.
summary: A 54-year-old male with COPD, hypertension, reflux and high cholesterol attended pulmonology follow-up for breathlessness on stairs and a morning cough with white phlegm, with two flare-ups in the past year. He denied fever, chills, night sweats and chest pain, and takes fish oil, vitamin D (corrected to 2,000 units daily) and a licorice-containing herbal capsule. Oxygen saturation was 94%, post-bronchodilator FEV1 was 52% of predicted and eosinophils were 320. Anoro Ellipta was changed to Trelegy Ellipta, omeprazole was increased to 40 mg, and the herbal capsule was stopped. Pulmonary rehabilitation, a yearly low-dose chest CT, a flu shot and a three-month return were arranged.

note:
Reason for consult: Evaluation and management of neutropenia in a patient receiving chemotherapy. Requesting service: emergency medicine.

HPI: 63-year-old female with breast cancer, 10 days after cycle 3 of docetaxel 75 mg/m2 and cyclophosphamide 600 mg/m2 given every three weeks, who came to the emergency department with 2 days of fatigue and a sore mouth. She did not receive growth factor support with the prior cycles. She has been eating less because of mouth soreness but is tolerating liquids. She denies fever, chills, cough, dysuria, diarrhea, and rash. No sick contacts.

Pertinent history: Breast cancer on adjuvant chemotherapy through a right chest port. Hypertension on amlodipine 5 mg daily. No known drug allergies.

Exam: Temp 99.1 F, BP 118/70, HR 92, RR 16, SpO2 98% on room air. Fatigued but nontoxic and in no distress. Mild grade 1 oral mucositis of the buccal mucosa without thrush or ulceration. Port site is clean with no erythema or tenderness. Lungs clear. Abdomen soft and nontender. No rash.

Data reviewed: WBC 1.1 with ANC 480, hemoglobin 10.4, platelets 142, creatinine 0.8. Lactate normal. Urinalysis negative. Chest x-ray clear. Blood cultures from the port and a peripheral vein are pending.

Impression: Chemotherapy-induced neutropenia, grade 3, after docetaxel and cyclophosphamide, afebrile and hemodynamically stable with no identified source of infection. Mild oral mucositis. Hypertension, stable.

Recommendations:
- Give the first dose of filgrastim 300 mcg subcutaneously in the ED, then daily at home until ANC recovers above 1500, with self-injection teaching.
- Reasonable to discharge home with neutropenic precautions if she remains afebrile on observation and blood cultures stay negative.
- Repeat CBC with differential in 48 hours at the infusion center.
- Hold the next cycle until ANC is above 1500 and reduce docetaxel to 60 mg/m2.
- Salt and baking soda mouth rinses four times daily.
- Return immediately for a temperature of 100.4 F or higher, or shaking chills.
- Continue amlodipine 5 mg daily.
- Oncology clinic follow-up within one week.
summary: A 63-year-old female with breast cancer on docetaxel and cyclophosphamide presented to the emergency department with fatigue and a sore mouth, and oncology was consulted. She denied fever, chills, cough, dysuria, diarrhea and rash, and she was afebrile with mild oral mucositis, WBC 1.1 and ANC 480. The impression was grade 3 chemotherapy-induced neutropenia without an identified source of infection, with stable hypertension. Filgrastim was started, with a repeat CBC in 48 hours, the next cycle held until ANC recovers with docetaxel reduced to 60 mg/m2, mouth rinses, return precautions for fever, and oncology follow-up within a week.

note:
Telehealth video visit, patient at home with good audio and video, for a 76-year-old male with right hand numbness. History is patient-reported, with a limited visual exam over video.

He reports numbness and tingling in the right thumb, index, and middle fingers for about four months, worse at night and waking him from sleep two to three times a week. He shakes the hand to relieve it. He also notes a weaker grip and has dropped a coffee cup twice. He denies neck pain, denies weakness of the whole arm, denies a recent injury, and denies numbness in the left hand.

History includes type 2 diabetes and hypertension. Current medications are metformin 500 mg twice daily, lisinopril 10 mg daily, and ibuprofen 400 mg three times a day that he has been taking over the counter for hand pain. Home readings: BP 136/80 with a home cuff, pulse 72, and fasting glucose 128 this morning.

Transportation: He no longer drives and lives about 45 minutes from the clinic. He relies on a neighbor or a senior shuttle that runs only a few days a week, which makes in-person visits hard.

Limited video exam: Alert, in no distress, speaking in full sentences. No visible swelling, redness, or deformity of the right wrist. No visible thenar atrophy. He can make a full fist and oppose the thumb to each fingertip. With guidance he did the Phalen maneuver for 30 seconds and reproduced tingling in the thumb, index, and middle fingers, and self-tapping over the carpal tunnel produced tingling as well. Sensation and strength could not be formally tested over video.

Impression: Right carpal tunnel syndrome, likely related in part to his type 2 diabetes, a clinical diagnosis from history and provocative maneuvers. Hypertension is stable on home readings. NSAID use is not ideal with lisinopril and his age.

Recommendations: Stop ibuprofen and use acetaminophen 650 mg every 6 hours as needed. A prefabricated neutral wrist splint will be mailed to his home, to be worn at night and during aggravating activities. Order nerve conduction studies and EMG of the right arm; the clinic will bundle these with an in-person visit on the same day, and our social worker will arrange medical transportation assistance. If symptoms persist after six weeks of splinting, a corticosteroid injection could be done at that same in-person visit. Continue metformin and lisinopril. Telehealth follow-up in six weeks. Return sooner for worsening weakness, constant numbness, or muscle wasting in the hand.

Nurse: The patient is a 58-year-old female here for a skin check, mostly about rough spots on her scalp and forearms. Blood pressure 132/78, pulse 70.

Doctor: Hello, nice to meet you. Tell me about the rough spots.

Patient: They're scaly, kind of sandpaper-like, on the tops of my forearms and a few on my scalp. They've been there maybe a year and seem to be getting more numerous.

Doctor: Do they hurt, itch, or bleed?

Patient: They sting a bit when I'm in the sun, but no itching and no bleeding.

Doctor: Any sore that won't heal, or a spot that has grown quickly?

Patient: No, nothing like that. No new moles either.

Doctor: Tell me about your sun exposure.

Patient: I garden every weekend and I've always burned easily. I use sunscreen sometimes, honestly not every time.

Doctor: Any personal history of skin cancer?

Patient: No.

Doctor: What medicines do you take?

Patient: Hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg once a day and atorvastatin 20 mg at night.

Doctor: Okay. Last visit I did a shave biopsy of the thick spot on your left temple. That came back as a hypertrophic actinic keratosis with no sign of squamous cell carcinoma, so that is good news.

Patient: What a relief.

Doctor: On exam today you have about a dozen rough, erythematous scaly patches on both forearms and six on the scalp, and the left temple biopsy site is healed. None are ulcerated or tender, and I see no suspicious pigmented lesions on your face, arms, or back. This confirms actinic keratoses from long-term sun damage.

Patient: Can we get rid of them?

Doctor: Yes. Today I'll freeze the scalp spots with liquid nitrogen, which will sting for a moment and then crust over for a week or two. For the forearms there are too many to freeze, so I'm starting fluorouracil 5% cream, applied twice a day to both forearms for three weeks. Your skin will get red, raw, and crusty, which means it is working. Use acetaminophen if it is sore, and avoid sun on the treated skin. Please wear SPF 50 sunscreen every day and a wide-brimmed hat when gardening. Hydrochlorothiazide can make your skin more sensitive to the sun, so I'll let your primary doctor know. I'd like to see you in six weeks, and then a full skin check once a year.

Patient: Okay, that makes sense.
summary: A 58-year-old female presented to dermatology with a year of scaly, rough spots on the forearms and scalp that sting in the sun without itching or bleeding. She gardens often, burns easily and uses sunscreen inconsistently. A shave biopsy of a thick left temple lesion at the last visit showed hypertrophic actinic keratosis without squamous cell carcinoma, and today about a dozen forearm and six scalp patches were diagnosed as actinic keratoses. The scalp lesions were frozen with liquid nitrogen and fluorouracil 5% cream twice a day for three weeks was started for the forearms. She was given sun protection advice, follow-up in six weeks and yearly skin checks.

note:
Nurse: This is a 45-year-old female with known multiple sclerosis, here with numbness and weakness in her left leg for four days. Blood pressure 124/76, heart rate 80, temp 98.4, oxygen sat 99% on room air.

Doctor: Hi there. Tell me what has been going on.

Patient: Four days ago my left foot started tingling, and it has crept up to my hip. Now the leg feels heavy and it drags when I walk. I'm also exhausted.

Doctor: Is that how your relapses have felt before?

Patient: Yes, this is just like the one I had three years ago, when my right leg went numb.

Doctor: Any vision changes, double vision, or eye pain?

Patient: No, my vision is fine.

Doctor: Any trouble controlling your bladder or bowels?

Patient: No. No accidents.

Doctor: Burning with urination, fever, or chills?

Patient: None of that.

Doctor: Any back injury or back pain?

Patient: No, no back pain.

Doctor: What medications are you on?

Patient: Dimethyl fumarate 240 mg twice a day for the MS, and baclofen 10 mg three times a day for leg stiffness. No medication allergies.

Doctor: Thanks. On exam, your cranial nerves and vision are normal. Strength is 4 out of 5 in the left hip flexor and ankle dorsiflexion, and normal on the right. You have reduced pinprick sensation in the left leg below the hip, and the reflexes are brisker at the left knee. Your gait is mildly unsteady but you can walk without help. Your urine test here is negative for infection, your white count is 6.2, and your blood sugar is 104, so this does not look like an infection making your old symptoms flare. This is consistent with a multiple sclerosis relapse.

Patient: What do we do about it?

Doctor: We treat relapses with high-dose steroids. I'm giving you the first dose of methylprednisolone 1000 mg IV here today, and the infusion center will give you the next two doses on the following two days. I'm also starting pantoprazole 40 mg once daily while you are on steroids to protect your stomach. Keep taking the dimethyl fumarate and baclofen. We need an MRI of the brain and cervical and thoracic spine with and without contrast, and I'll have your neurologist's office see you within a week. Steroids can raise your blood sugar and affect your sleep. Go to the emergency room right away if you lose vision, if the weakness spreads, or if you can't pass urine.

Patient: Okay, I understand.

Examination showed 4 out of 5 left hip flexor and ankle strength, reduced pinprick sensation in the left leg and brisker left knee reflexes, and the urine test was negative for infection. The diagnosis was a multiple sclerosis relapse. She received the first dose of methylprednisolone 1000 mg IV, will complete two more doses at the infusion center, started pantoprazole, and will have an MRI and neurology review within a week.

78-year-old female seen in the geriatrics clinic for unintentional weight loss and declining strength. She lives alone and reports that over the past six months her appetite has dropped and she now eats mostly one full meal a day, with tea and toast otherwise. She says shopping and cooking have become tiring. She has lost about 5 kg without trying and says her clothes are loose. She denies dysphagia, denies nausea, denies abdominal pain, denies diarrhea, and denies night sweats. Mood is described as okay and her PHQ-2 score is 1. She has hypertension, treated with amlodipine 5 mg daily.

On examination she looks thin and frail but is alert and pleasant. Weight is 54.6 kg, down from 59.8 kg six months ago, which is about a 9% loss. Blood pressure is 128/74 and heart rate 68. Oral exam shows poorly fitting upper dentures, with no thrush or ulcers. Heart and lungs are normal, and the abdomen is soft and nontender with no masses. Gait speed is slow at 0.7 meters per second and grip strength is reduced. Labs from last week show hemoglobin 11.8, TSH 2.2, and creatinine 0.9.

My impression is frailty with unintentional weight loss, most likely from reduced oral intake related to poor dentition, living alone, and age-related decline, with no alarming features on today's evaluation. I recommended an oral nutrition supplement twice daily between meals, referral to a dietitian and to home-delivered meals, a dental referral for her dentures, and physical therapy for strength and balance. We will order a chest x-ray to complete the evaluation. Continue amlodipine. She will return in four weeks for a weight check.

Nurse: This is a 56-year-old male on chemotherapy for colon cancer. His oncology office sent him in after routine labs showed a low white count. Temp 98.9, blood pressure 126/78, heart rate 88, oxygen sat 98% on room air.

Doctor: Hello. How are you feeling?

Patient: Tired, mostly. My mouth is a little sore too. I had my FOLFOX ten days ago, and I get it every two weeks.

Doctor: Any fever or chills?

Patient: No fever, no chills. I checked my temperature twice today.

Doctor: Any cough, burning with urination, or diarrhea?

Patient: None of those.

Doctor: Let me look. Your mouth looks mildly red with no white patches, your lungs are clear, your belly is soft, and there is no redness around your port. Your blood count came back with a white count of 1.9 and an absolute neutrophil count of 600, which is low. That is chemotherapy-induced neutropenia. Since you have no fever and look well, you can go home. I spoke with the on-call oncologist, and they want a repeat blood count in three days and will decide about a growth factor shot.

Patient: What should I watch for?

Doctor: Check your temperature twice a day, and don't take Tylenol before checking it. Wash your hands often and stay away from sick people. Go to the emergency room right away if your temperature is 100.4 or higher, or if you have shaking chills. Call the oncology office in the morning.

Patient: Okay.

summary: An 85-year-old female on hospital day 5 for acute on chronic diastolic heart failure was seen by geriatrics for advance care planning; she was anxious and asked many questions about resuscitation, machines and her daily wine. Her history includes HFpEF, AFib, CKD stage 3b, T2DM and knee OA, with heavy alcohol use and no withdrawal. She first said she took only Tylenol, but her daughter's bottle showed Advil 400 mg TID. With capacity intact she chose DNR/DNI, named her daughter as surrogate and completed a POLST. Advil was stopped, apixaban was reduced to 2.5 mg BID, and palliative care referral and follow-up were arranged.

soap.subjective: 85-year-old female, hospital day 5, admitted with acute on chronic diastolic HF and now near euvolemic, seen for advance care planning at the request of the primary team with her daughter at the bedside. Very anxious and asked many questions (what if her heart stops, will she be on a machine, can she still have her wine, who decides if she can't talk); answered in plain language and she was calmer by the end. No events overnight; CIWA 2 to 0 with no withdrawal symptoms. Denies chest pain, shortness of breath at rest, orthopnea, tremor, hallucinations, seizure, nausea or vomiting, and melena. Reports knee pain from OA. History of HFpEF, AFib, CKD stage 3b, T2DM, OA of the knees, and heavy alcohol use (about 4 glasses of wine daily for many years, last drink before admission). Widowed, lives alone with her daughter nearby, denies tobacco. Medications: furosemide 40 mg PO daily, apixaban 5 mg BID, metoprolol succinate 25 mg daily, glipizide 5 mg daily, thiamine 100 mg and folic acid 1 mg daily started on admission, and acetaminophen 500 mg every 6 hours as needed. She first said she took only Tylenol for her knees, corrected when her daughter brought in the bottle: she takes Advil 400 mg TID for months.
soap.objective: BP 118/66, HR 72, RR 18, Temp 98.1 F, SpO2 95% on room air; weight down 2 kg from admission. Frail, thin, alert and oriented x3. JVP flat, lungs clear, trace leg edema, no tremor, no asterixis. Na 136, K 4.3, Cr 1.6 (baseline 1.5), eGFR 31, Hgb 10.9, MCV 102, platelets 160, INR 1.2, AST 52, ALT 31, albumin 3.3, A1c 7.4. Echo this admission: EF 55%, grade II diastolic dysfunction. CXR: small bilateral effusions, improving.
soap.assessment: Advance care planning completed: the patient has capacity, chose DNR/DNI with full treatment otherwise, named her daughter as health care surrogate, and completed a POLST. HFpEF, compensated. AFib with age and Cr 1.6 prompting apixaban dose reduction. CKD stage 3b with NSAID exposure, so ibuprofen is stopped. Heavy alcohol use with macrocytosis and mild AST elevation, no withdrawal. T2DM with A1c 7.4, acceptable for age. OA of the knees.

Doctor: Welcome. I'm seeing a 70-year-old female for recurrent urinary tract infections. Tell me what has been happening.

Patient: I've had three bladder infections in the last six months. Each time I get burning when I urinate and I have to go all the time. My primary doctor gave me antibiotics and it clears up, then it comes back.

Doctor: Did the urine cultures show a germ?

Patient: Yes, E. coli every time, I think.

Doctor: Any fever, back pain, or blood in the urine that you can see?

Patient: No fever, no back pain, and I haven't seen blood.

Doctor: Do you leak urine or have trouble emptying your bladder?

Patient: No leaking, and I empty fine.

Doctor: What medicines do you take?

Patient: Apixaban 5 mg twice a day for my atrial fibrillation. That's the only one. No allergies.

Doctor: Good. Your urine today shows no infection, but there are a few red blood cells under the microscope. Your bladder scan after urinating shows only 20 mL left, so you are emptying well. On exam you have thin, dry vaginal tissue, which is common after menopause and makes infections more likely.

Patient: What can we do?

Doctor: I recommend vaginal estradiol cream, 0.5 gram twice a week at bedtime, which helps protect against infections. Keep taking apixaban 5 mg twice a day and drink plenty of water. Because of the blood in the urine, I'm ordering a kidney and bladder ultrasound and a cystoscopy to look inside the bladder. Your blood thinner can cause bleeding, but it should not be the only explanation, so we need to check. Come back in three months, or sooner if you have another infection.

Patient: That sounds fine.
summary: A 70-year-old female with atrial fibrillation on apixaban was seen in urology for three bladder infections in six months, each with burning and frequent urination and E. coli on culture by her recollection. She denied fever, back pain, visible blood, leaking and trouble emptying her bladder. Today's urine showed no infection but a few red blood cells, the bladder scan showed 20 mL left after voiding, and the exam showed thin, dry vaginal tissue. The diagnosis was recurrent urinary tract infections, and vaginal estradiol cream twice a week was started, apixaban continued, and a kidney and bladder ultrasound and cystoscopy ordered, with follow-up in three months.
